readerTitle: What a lost deal is still worth
caseNote: 가상 사례 (주방용품 유통사와 식료품 체인, 사내 데이터팀) · 모든 수치와 확률은 설명용 가정
insight: 진 거래는 끝이 아니라 다음 거래의 시작이다. 지는 순간의 행동이 그 거래의 남은 가치를 정한다.
misconception: 진 거래는 가치가 0이다. 그러니 마지막 할인으로 붙잡거나, 아니면 바로 잊고 넘어가야 한다.

sources.text: 영업 실무의 일반 개념 (win-loss review, 실주 후 관계 관리)
모든 수치와 확률은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 기대값 계산: 재계약 시점에 돌아올 확률 1/4은 실제 통계가 아니라 설명용 가정입니다. 0.25 × $50,000 = 연 $12,500. 카드 문장에도 'suppose'로 가정임을 밝혔습니다.
'결정이 끝난 뒤 구매자가 더 솔직하게 이유를 말한다'는 주장은 연구 수치 없이 일반적 관찰로만 표현했습니다. 단정적 표현으로 바뀌지 않았는지 게시 전 확인하세요.

cards.title: The buyer just said no. The deal isn't over.
body: A kitchen-supply distributor spent four months pitching a 12-store grocery chain. The account was worth $200,000 a year in sales.
Yesterday the buyer chose a rival that was 8% cheaper and signed a two-year contract. What the sales rep does in the next ten minutes decides what this "no" is worth.

image.label: A sales rep on the phone outside a grocery store
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 식료품 매장 하역장 앞에서 영업 담당자가 전화를 들고 서 있고, 옆에 주방용품 상자가 쌓인 배송 트럭. 표정은 실망보다 침착함. 실제 매장·브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You've lost. What now?
body: The buyer calls to say they're going with the other distributor. The contract is signed. Your margin on the account would have been 25%.
What do you do on this call?

options.text: Offer to beat the rival's price by 8% if they reconsider
options.feedback: It might reopen the door, but it tells the buyer your first price was padded. And even if it works, you keep far less than you think.

options.text: Thank them politely and move on to the next lead
options.feedback: You stay on good terms and save time. But you learn nothing, and you leave no reason to talk again.

options.text: Accept it, ask what decided it, offer a smooth handover and ask to check in before renewal
options.feedback: You give up the deal for now but keep the relationship, the lesson and a reason to return. The next cards put numbers on that.

cards.title: Saving it with a discount costs a third of the profit.
body: An 8% price cut comes entirely out of your margin. Profit falls from $50,000 to **$34,000** a year, a 32% drop, on an account the buyer now knows you'll discount.

cards.title: Losing a deal well
body: **Losing a deal well** means treating the lost deal as the start of the next conversation. You accept the decision, learn the real reason, make the switch easy and keep a reason to come back.
A desperate save trades profit for a deal. A burned bridge trades the future for a moment of frustration. Losing well trades a few hours for options.

image.label: Three doors: slammed, closed, left open
image.brief: 문 세 개를 나란히 그린 일러스트. 첫째 문은 쾅 닫힘("Burned bridge"), 둘째는 조용히 닫힘("Moved on"), 셋째는 살짝 열려 빛이 새어 나옴("Lost well"). 셋째 문을 강조.

cards.title: The lost account still has a value.
body: Suppose that, if you leave well, there's a 1 in 4 chance the chain comes back when the rival's contract ends. If you leave badly, that chance is close to zero. The open door is worth about **$12,500** a year in expected profit, before counting referrals and lessons.

breakdown.label: Assumed chance
breakdown.detail: If you left on good terms

breakdown.label: Expected value
breakdown.detail: Per year, for a few hours of effort

cards.title: Why the moment after "no" matters most.
body: Once the decision is made, the pressure is gone. Buyers often speak more honestly about why you lost: price, delivery times, or a rep who didn't listen.
A smooth handover is remembered. If the rival stumbles, the buyer knows who to call. And buyers change jobs. The one you treated well may run purchasing somewhere else next year.
cards.softwareNote: When a trial user or prospect says no, ask one short question about why, make it easy to export their data, and keep them on a light update list. People who could leave easily tend to remember it when they reconsider.

cards.title: Losing well is not giving up early.
body: Fight hard while the decision is still open. Losing well starts only after the buyer has decided.

Don't turn the "why did we lose?" question into a disguised re-pitch. And don't chase every lost account forever. Check in at natural moments, like before a renewal, and keep your effort in proportion to what the account could be worth.

cards.title: Now it's a team inside your company.
body: You lead the in-house analytics team. You pitched to run a customer study for the marketing department. Marketing chose an outside agency instead.

options.text: Ask your VP to overrule marketing and give you the project
options.feedback: You might win this project, but marketing will remember being overruled. Future work may stop coming to you at all.

options.text: Ask what tipped the choice, hand the agency your existing data, and offer a check-in at the halfway mark
options.feedback: You lose this project but learn what marketing values and become the helpful option if the agency falls short.

options.text: Stay quiet and wait for the agency to struggle
options.feedback: You may get called back if things go wrong. But slow help looks like a grudge, and you learn nothing about why you lost.

cards.title: How you lose decides what the loss is worth.
body: A lost deal isn't zero. Accept it, learn why, make the switch easy and keep a reason to return.
**Try it today:** pick one deal you lost this year. Send a short note asking what decided it, with no pitch attached.
